records.name: Madagascar
records.current_summary: Madagascar demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal — unusual for the region — but France 24 documents that LGBT people must hide to keep jobs and live in peace; there is no LGR, no anti-discrimination law, and no visible community outside Antananarivo. No documented police targeting pattern.
records.current_outOfScope: Thin data; legal but closeted profile.

sources.claim: France 24 'Focus' report (Aug 2024): 'LGBT people in Madagascar forced to hide their sexuality' — although homosexuality is not illegal, it is widely considered socially unacceptable; many hide to keep jobs and live in peace, developing their own networks and coded language.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Madagascar: documents the post-coup regime, unlawful killings, and 'societal discrimination and violence against women, persons with disabilities, and the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community'.

BBC News Pidgin overview of decriminalisation in Africa (July 2020): Madagascar entry — same-sex activity legal only from age 21 under the Penal Code (under-21 same-sex acts remain offences); no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions; regional context as ~22 of 53 African states had moved to decriminalise.

Queer In The World Madagascar guide (updated 3 December 2023): same-sex activity legal for over-21s but LGBT people face discrimination and lack civic rights such as marriage and adoption; the legal framework is limited in progress compared with other countries.

Erasing 76 Crimes (17 July 2025): in Madagascar’s fourth UPR (January 2025, 235 recommendations) the government rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent; six Malagasy organisations (Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers’ Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage, Madagascar LGBT+) protested that "Refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence."

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Madagascar resources: Penal Code Article 331 sets a different age of consent for same-sex acts (indecent-assault band of five to ten years’ imprisonment); documents general societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ people plus state-protection capacity, case law and supporting organisations.

records.name: Guinea-Bissau
records.current_summary: Guinea-Bissau demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (one of few West African states never to criminalise); no LGR, no protections; chronic instability (coups) and weak state; documented social hostility but no mob-lynching pattern of Benin's type.

sources.claim: US State Dept 2012 report on Guinea-Bissau: documents the 2012 coup, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and impunity; notes no criminalisation of same-sex conduct — general security context for visitors.
US State Dept 2011 report: security-force torture, FGM and impunity documented; the LGBT section notes no criminalisation but societal stigma against LGBT people.

Overview of LGBT rights in Guinea-Bissau: same-sex conduct legal since 1993 (penal code decree 4/93 omits same-sex offences); signed the 2008 UN SOGI statement; only married heterosexual couples entitled to larger government housing; domestic-violence law (6/2014) Article 5 protects victims regardless of sexual orientation.
LiquiSearch: LGBT rights in Guinea-Bissau - brief overview page (Wikipedia-derived) noting legal challenges and sections on same-sex activity, relationships, adoption and living conditions.

Mapa.gay country guide for Guinea-Bissau: legal since 1993; no partnership recognition; no trans framework; travel-safety score 34/100 ('Caution'); 9% consider homosexual behaviour morally acceptable — unusually moderate for West Africa; no visible LGBT scene; some violence cases (2018).

freshness_all.fact: Legal since 1993, no relationship recognition or protections — current overview still says exactly that; cited 2009-2017 reports' legal baseline unchanged (social-stigma framing remains apt).

records.name: North Korea
records.current_summary: North Korea is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Same-sex conduct is not named in the Criminal Code — but Article 193 prohibits “decadent culture,” and broad provisions on obscene activities give authorities unlimited discretion; reported incidents of criminalisation and even execution for homosexuality exist. The concept of gender identity simply does not exist in public life (BBC Korea: sexual minorities are “denied as a concept”). Tourists are under constant escort and surveillance; any nonconforming presentation or discovered digital material risks detention in the world's most totalitarian system.
records.current_outOfScope: Data scarcity reflects totalitarian control; traveler surveillance is universal.

sources.claim: Outright International country page (updated 12 Mar 2026): DPRK Criminal Code (1950, rev. 2009) appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts, but Art. 193 bans import/keeping/distribution of 'decadent culture' incl. sexual recordings and Art. 262 bans collective 'obscene activities'; 2014 KCNA denied homosexuality's existence; an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017; no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people; no registration route for LGBTI orgs.

Legal Clarity overview: sex-marker change on birth certificate/citizen card technically possible under 'unavoidable circumstances' - application to People's Security Agency plus state forensic medical evaluation, in practice requiring surgical intervention; no law explicitly bans gender-affirming care but the under-resourced health system makes hormones/surgery effectively inaccessible.

BBC Korean feature (10 Oct 2024), 'Does homosexuality exist in North Korea too?': 10 years after the UN COI report, new laws (Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act etc.) tighten control; profiles Jang Young-jin, a novelist who defected in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed, as the first publicly known gay defector; documents how a collective-over-individual regime forces DPRK sexual minorities into silent self-suppression and frames LGBT life as human-rights abuse.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for North Korea: official assessment - the totalitarian regime's pervasive abuses; the report notes no specific law criminalising same-sex conduct but the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life.

US State Department 2020 Human Rights Report for North Korea: official assessment - no reliable information on LGBT persons; the regime's repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality.
CNN (Apr 2017): 'I could not even dream: Life as a gay North Korean' — a defector's account of homosexuality's place in North Korean society and its punishment.

KCNA commentary (22 Apr 2014): state news agency rejects the UN Commission of Inquiry's DPRK human rights report as a political fabrication and personally attacks commissioner Michael Kirby as 'a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality' to discredit it - official-record evidence of the regime's hostility toward homosexuality even while denying its existence.

records.name: Palestinian Territories
records.current_summary: The Palestinian Territories are dangerous for trans visitors, with a hard internal split. In the West Bank, same-sex conduct is not criminalised (1951 Jordanian code) but there are no protections, family/clan hostility is severe, and LGBT Palestinians flee to Israel for safety (Israeli courts now grant such asylum claims). In Gaza, a British Mandate law technically allows 10 years, Hamas has executed people for alleged homosexuality, and the territory is in a catastrophic war. Cairo 52 notes trans identities are not explicitly criminalised but gender-affirming healthcare is essentially destroyed/unavailable.
records.current_localsOnly: The destroyed/unavailable gender-affirming healthcare and the family/clan hostility dynamics describe residents' situation; the asylum-flight pattern to Israel is a resident phenomenon.
records.current_outOfScope: West Bank/Gaza scored as one de jure unit; Gaza is far worse in practice (war + Hamas).

sources.claim: CAIRO 51 Palestine page: Gaza (British Mandate Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936 still in force, silent on trans identities but trans people potentially caught by public-morality provisions) vs West Bank have different penal codes; pinkwashing critique - occupation marginalises queer/trans Palestinians alongside everyone else; documented de facto oppression.

Legal Clarity: West Bank criminal law derives from the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960 - Jordan's 1951 revision dropped consensual-private-sex offences and the 1960 code carried that forward; practical reality harsher than formal law via social/family persecution. Formal-decognition map for West Bank.

Wikipedia LGBT rights in Palestine: patchwork decriminalisation (British Mandate code in Jordan until 1951; Jordanian Penal Code no prohibition of same-sex acts applied to the West Bank; Israel stopped using the code in 1977); PA has not legislated; no explicit prohibition on trans identity; periodic transphobic threats/attacks; PA a non-signatory to key treaties.

HRW 'Audacity of Adversity' (16 Apr 2018): LGBT people across MENA finding ways to speak out - stories, cross-border alliances, national/regional movements combating homophobia and transphobia; accompanies AFE video series of activist messages of support. Regional movement context for Palestinian LGBT life.

Times of Israel: rights groups slammed Palestinian police for banning LGBTQ activity - after the police action against al-Qaws, the foundation received a wave of hate messages which activists said 'pose a serious threat' to the gay community.

HRW (11 Jun 2018), Women's Centre for Legal Aid: interviewed 12 Palestinian women identifying as lesbian/bisexual/queer - widespread discrimination and abuse in public and family settings; Gaza's 1936 Criminal Code s.152(2) punishes consensual same-sex 'carnal knowledge' by up to 10 years (vague 'unnatural offences' concepts violate privacy/non-discrimination per HRW); 1960 West Bank code analysed similarly.

Times of Israel: Israel to allow LGBT Palestinians granted temporary asylum to work - some 90 LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence in the territories.

records.name: Gibraltar
records.current_summary:
Gibraltar legislates its own civil and criminal law as a self-governing territory on the Iberian peninsula's southern tip. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1993 with an equal age of consent since 2012; discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment date from 2007; civil partnerships followed in 2014, and same-sex marriage was enacted unanimously in December 2016 after a 2015 public consultation returned overwhelming support (3,490 replies from a 24,117-person electorate).

For a transgender visitor the standing gap is legal gender: no route exists to change legal gender, and there was no specific hate-crime provision denigrating a person for sexual orientation until, in July 2021, the Ministry for Justice said it would 'urgently' consider one after a wave of online homophobia during Pride month drew a rare public rebuke from the head of government. Governance of the territory is subject to regular scrutiny by the UK parliament's overseas-territories committee, which has pressed accountability standards across the portfolio.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee, Seventh Report (2007-08) on Overseas Territories: governance chapter - covers good-governance expectations, corruption concerns (Turks and Caicos), and accountability issues across the territories including Gibraltar.

El País in English (15 Aug 2016): Gibraltar put a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act for same-sex marriage before Parliament after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarized; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, with popular consultation and main parties suggesting support for the change.

Gibraltar Chronicle (22 Jul 2021): the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar - legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by Supreme Court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since Dec 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and 'gender reassignment' since 2007; transgender persons not allowed to change legal gender.

freshness_all.fact: Legal since 1993, equal age of consent 2012, civil pacts 2014, same-sex marriage since 2016, SO+gender-reassignment protections since 2007; no legal gender recognition

records.name: Bermuda
records.current_summary:
Bermuda decriminalised private adult same-sex conduct in 1994 (House of Assembly, 22-16) and in 2013 outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriages performed in 2017 were withdrawn the following year by a Domestic Partnership Act — the first jurisdiction anywhere to reverse marriage equality — and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld that restoration of the traditional-marriage definition, so partnerships, not marriage, are the available status for same-sex couples.

For a transgender visitor the more telling fact is the protection gap: there is no legal recognition of transgender people, and therefore no gender-identity-specific discrimination protection at all. Church influence is significant in local politics — when a prominent entertainer's gay-charity cruise sought to dock in 2007 the premier's colourful defence was needed against religious objections — and the tourism economy that the island depends on has repeatedly had to be pointed at inclusivity.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

Social climate: Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre' — organised religious hostility to visible same-sex couples.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections — a debate that split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

records.name: Cayman Islands
records.current_summary:
Cayman law never held the criminalisation its earlier profile asserted: same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature refused, albeit with an unequal age of consent surviving the reform. In 2020 the Court of Appeal held that a same-sex couple's overseas marriage must be recognised, and in July 2021 roughly 600 people — including the premier, the governor and other ministers — joined the islands' first Pride parade, one of the broadest official turnouts a community there has seen.

The sharp turn came in 2022: a statute confining family status to heterosexual marriage took effect and, in March of that year, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rejected the challenge to it. Same-sex couples therefore have no marriage or civil-partnership status, the country that administers defence and foreign affairs declined to force the issue, and equality advocates have operated mainly through immigration and recognition rulings rather than family law itself.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: PinkNews (11 Aug 2009): UK MPs on the Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave Cayman courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Art 14 requires; the FCO countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended. Early-dated evidence of London–local friction over LGBT protections that frames the later recognition rulings.

Cayman News Service (29 Jul 2021): around 600 people — including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs — joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade (Sat 7 Aug 2021 debut), an historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection (organisers' condition amid public-space sensitivities). Evidence of high official tolerance in the tourist-facing environment.

Washington Blade (30 Dec 2020): immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder (wed in Ireland), the Court of Appeal holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds; recaps that Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie had struck down the same-sex marriage ban in March 2019 (later overturned on appeal, Aug 2019 — the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived). Core source for the 'recognition without status' travel posture.

records.name: British Virgin Islands
records.current_summary:
Same-sex intimacy in the British Virgin Islands was decriminalised in January 2001 by order of the administering state's Privy Council, after the local legislature refused to act — a local legislator's 'there is nothing we can do about it' captured the resentment with which the reform landed. Family status remains contested rather than settled: in 2022 the Court of Appeal refused the local churches council's attempt to appeal a judgment in favour of two women, married in the UK, who were seeking recognition of their marriage and a declaration that the prohibition is unconstitutional — the court finding the proposed appeal had no realistic prospect of success.

Visitors encounter a tolerant-but-quiet society: travel surveys rate these twin islands among the more gay-welcoming in the Caribbean while noting resistance beneath the surface, with most local hostility 'silent and invisible' and most visitors hardly noticing either way. Discretion, not danger, is the operative norm.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: AP report (Jan 2001) republished by GLAPN: Britain scrapped the homosexuality laws in its five remaining Caribbean territories -- including the British Virgin Islands -- by Privy Council order after local legislatures refused to act; local legislator Orlando Smith conceded 'there is nothing we can do' -- the decriminalisation moment for this territory.

GlobalGayz profile (Aug 2012/2017): the BVI is among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean but with 'silent and invisible' native homophobia and secret lives -- undated snapshot of the social climate for gay visitors.

BVI News (29 Jul 2022): the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal case-management orders (Justice Adrian Jack) in the case testing recognition of the UK same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome -- litigation over whether same-sex marriages are valid under BVI law.
